1. Transaction Processing Systems (TPS):

A Transaction Processing System (TPS) is a computerised system that captures, validates,
records, and processes the routine, day-to-day business transactions of an organisation - such
as sales, purchases, payroll runs, and bank deposits - forming the operational foundation on
which every higher-level information system in the enterprise depends.

Fig: Functional Area Information Systems Drawing on Shared Transaction Data
Explanation:
Before enterprise-wide integration became common, each department in an organisation often
built or purchased its own dedicated system tailored precisely to its own workflows: a
marketing and sales information system to track leads, campaigns, and sales performance; a
finance and accounting information system to manage the general ledger, accounts payable
and receivable, and financial reporting; a manufacturing and operations information system to
schedule production, monitor machine utilisation, and control quality; and a human resources
information system to manage employee records and payroll.
Each functional area system draws on the same underlying transaction data - a sale recorded by
the TPS is relevant to both the marketing system (as a completed conversion) and the finance
system (as revenue to be recognised) - but transforms that shared data into the specific reports,
dashboards, and decision-support tools that matter to that particular department, rather than
presenting the same raw data to every user regardless of their role.
The major limitation of building functional area systems independently is data fragmentation:
when each department maintains its own separate database, the same customer or product
information can end up duplicated, inconsistently formatted, or simply out of sync between
departments. This exact limitation is the primary reason organisations later moved toward
Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems, which integrate functional area needs around
one shared database rather than many separate ones.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Tailored to departmental needs: Each system is optimised for the specific workflows,
terminology, and reporting requirements of its own department.
• Faster departmental decision-making: Staff get quick access to the specific metrics
and reports relevant to their role without wading through irrelevant enterprise-wide
data.

• Easier to implement individually: A single functional area system is typically smaller
in scope and can be deployed faster and more cheaply than a full enterprise-wide
system.
• Specialised functionality: Departmental systems can include deep, specialised features
(for example, detailed shop-floor scheduling in manufacturing) that a generic enterprise
system might not fully support.
• Clear departmental ownership: Each department can manage and customise its own
system according to its own priorities without needing enterprise-wide consensus.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Data silos and duplication: The same information (customer, product, or employee
data) can be stored inconsistently across multiple separate systems, leading to
conflicting records.
• Limited cross-department visibility: It becomes difficult to get a single, unified view
of the business when each department's data lives in a separate system.
• Costly integration efforts: Connecting or reconciling data across many independent
functional systems requires additional middleware, manual reconciliation, or custom
integration work.
• Inconsistent reporting: Two departments analysing what should be the same
underlying event can produce different figures if their systems process or define the data
differently.
• Redundant infrastructure costs: Maintaining multiple separate systems (licensing,
hosting, support) is often more expensive overall than one integrated platform.
Examples:
• Example 1: Marketing and sales system. A marketing information system tracks a
campaign's leads and conversions, generating a report on cost per acquisition for the
marketing team's review.
• Example 2: Finance and accounting system. The same sales transaction, once
completed, flows into the finance system, which records the resulting revenue in the
appropriate ledger account for the month's financial statements.
• Example 3: Manufacturing system. A manufacturing information system uses order
data to schedule production runs, allocating machine time and raw materials to meet the
confirmed order quantity by its deadline.
Applications:
• Sales and marketing reporting: Tracking campaign performance, lead conversion,
and sales quotas.
• Financial management: Managing the general ledger, budgets, and financial statement
preparation.

Most ERP systems are organised as a suite of modules that can be implemented together or, in

Human Capital Management, Manufacturing and Production, Sales and Distribution,
Procurement, and Inventory and Warehouse Management. Each module is built to handle its
specific business function in depth, while remaining tightly integrated with every other module
through the shared database and a common set of master data (such as one authoritative
customer list or one authoritative product catalogue used by every module).
Implementing ERP is a major undertaking rather than a simple software installation: it
typically requires re-engineering existing business processes to match the ERP system's built￾in best-practice workflows (or, alternatively, customising the ERP software itself), migrating
and cleaning historical data from legacy systems, and extensive staff training, since employees
across every department must learn to work within the new integrated system rather than their
previous, department-specific tools.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Single source of truth: A shared database eliminates data duplication and
inconsistency between departments, since every module reads and writes the same
underlying records.
• Improved cross-department visibility: Management can see a real-time, unified view
of the entire business - sales, inventory, finance, and operations together - rather than
piecing together separate reports.
• Streamlined business processes: Automating handoffs between departments (for
example, sales order automatically triggering procurement) reduces manual re-entry
and processing delays.
• Regulatory and financial compliance support: Centralised, consistent financial data
makes audit trails and statutory reporting significantly easier to produce accurately.
• Scalability for growing organisations: A well-implemented ERP can support an
organisation's growth into new locations, product lines, or business units on the same
core platform.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• High implementation cost and duration: Large ERP implementations can take many
months or years and require substantial investment in software, consulting, and internal
staff time.
• Significant organisational disruption: Because ERP often requires redesigning
existing business processes, implementation can face strong internal resistance to
change.

Diagram:
Fig: Supply Chain Management - Material and Information Flow
Explanation:
A supply chain typically spans several linked stages: suppliers who provide raw materials or
components, procurement teams who source and purchase what is needed, manufacturing that
converts inputs into finished goods, warehousing and distribution that store and move
products, retailers who sell to end customers, and finally the customers themselves. SCM
systems coordinate the physical movement of goods forward through this chain while
simultaneously managing the flow of demand and order information backward from customers
toward suppliers, so that production and procurement decisions stay aligned with actual
demand.
Modern SCM relies heavily on visibility and forecasting: by sharing real-time data on
inventory levels, order status, and demand forecasts across every link in the chain,
organisations can reduce the 'bullwhip effect' - a well-documented phenomenon in which
small fluctuations in customer demand become amplified into much larger swings in orders as
they propagate backward through the supply chain, leading to costly overstocking or
stockouts.
Effective SCM systems typically integrate several capabilities: demand planning and
forecasting, procurement and supplier relationship management, inventory optimisation
across multiple warehouse locations, transportation and logistics management, and
increasingly, real-time tracking technologies such as barcode scanning, RFID tagging, and IoT
sensors that give continuous visibility into exactly where goods are at any point in the chain.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Reduced inventory and holding costs: Better demand visibility across the chain lets
organisations hold less safety stock while still meeting customer demand reliably.

organisations.

employment lifecycle, from the moment a candidate applies for a role through onboarding,
ongoing employment, performance reviews, promotions, and eventually exit. Rather than

slides.text:
maintaining separate spreadsheets or systems for recruitment, payroll, and performance
tracking, an HRIS links all of this data to one employee record, ensuring consistency and
reducing duplicate data entry.
Core HRIS functionality is typically organised into modules that each serve a specific stage or
aspect of the employment relationship. Recruitment and onboarding modules manage job
postings, applicant tracking, and new-hire paperwork. Payroll and benefits modules calculate
salaries, taxes, and deductions, and administer employee benefits enrolment. Performance
management modules track goal-setting, reviews, and ratings over time. Training and
development modules manage learning programmes and track certifications or skill
development. Employee self-service portals let staff view their own payslips, request leave, or
update personal details directly, reducing the administrative burden on HR staff.
Modern HRIS platforms increasingly incorporate analytics capabilities - sometimes called
people analytics or HR analytics - that use the accumulated employee data to identify trends
such as which factors correlate with employee turnover, which recruitment channels produce
the strongest long-term hires, or which teams show early signs of disengagement, turning the
HRIS from a purely administrative record-keeping tool into a genuine strategic decision￾support system for workforce planning.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Centralised, consistent employee data: A single authoritative employee record
eliminates the inconsistencies that arise from maintaining HR data across multiple
disconnected spreadsheets or systems.
• Reduced administrative workload: Automating routine tasks such as payroll
calculation and leave approval frees HR staff to focus on more strategic activities.
• Improved compliance and accuracy: Automated calculation of statutory deductions
and consistent record-keeping reduces the risk of payroll errors and regulatory non￾compliance.
• Employee self-service convenience: Employees can independently check payslips,
request leave, or update details without needing to contact HR directly for routine
matters.
• Data-driven workforce decisions: HR analytics built on accumulated HRIS data help
identify turnover risk, skills gaps, and recruitment effectiveness.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Sensitive data privacy risk: An HRIS holds highly sensitive personal, financial, and
health-related employee data, making strong security and access controls essential.
• High implementation and migration cost: Moving historical employee records
accurately from legacy systems into a new HRIS can be a lengthy and costly
undertaking.

Explanation:
Knowledge within an organisation is often distinguished into two types: explicit knowledge,
which can be clearly written down, documented, and easily shared (such as a standard
operating procedure or a technical manual), and tacit knowledge, which is harder to articulate
and is typically held in the experience, skills, and judgement of individual employees (such as
a seasoned technician's intuitive understanding of a machine's quirks). A key challenge for
knowledge management is converting valuable tacit knowledge into explicit, shareable form
wherever possible.
Knowledge management is best understood as a continuous cycle rather than a one-time
project. New knowledge is created (through problem-solving, research, or experience),
captured (documented in a usable form, such as a report, wiki page, or recorded discussion),
stored in a shared, searchable repository, shared and disseminated across the organisation
(through training, communities of practice, or simple access to the repository), and applied to
solve new problems or make decisions - and the outcomes and lessons from applying that
knowledge in turn generate new knowledge, feeding back into the start of the cycle.

A KMS typically combines several supporting technologies: a searchable central repository or
knowledge base, collaboration tools such as internal wikis, discussion forums, and shared
workspaces that let employees contribute and refine knowledge together, and increasingly,
intelligent search and recommendation features (sometimes AI-assisted) that surface the most
relevant existing knowledge to an employee at the moment they need it, rather than requiring
them to know exactly what to search for.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Preserves organisational knowledge: Capturing expertise in a shared system reduces
the risk of losing critical know-how when experienced employees leave the
organisation.
• Faster problem-solving: Employees can search existing solutions to similar past
problems instead of solving the same issue repeatedly from scratch.
• Improved consistency and quality: Shared best-practice documentation helps ensure
work is carried out to a consistent standard across teams and locations.
• Accelerated employee onboarding: New employees can learn from a well-organised
knowledge repository far faster than relying solely on informal mentoring.
• Supports innovation: Making existing knowledge easily discoverable helps
employees combine ideas across different areas of the organisation in new ways.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Difficult to capture tacit knowledge: Much of the most valuable expertise is hard to
fully document, since experienced employees often cannot easily articulate exactly how
they make certain judgements.
• Requires ongoing employee participation: A knowledge system is only useful if
employees consistently take the time to contribute and update it, which competes with
their regular workload.
• Risk of outdated or inaccurate content: Without active maintenance, a knowledge
repository can accumulate stale or incorrect information that misleads users.
• Information overload: A poorly organised repository with too much unstructured
content can make it harder, not easier, to find genuinely useful knowledge.
• Cultural resistance to sharing: In some organisational cultures, employees may be
reluctant to openly share expertise they see as giving them individual value or job
security.
Examples:
• Example 1: Internal technical wiki. A software company maintains an internal wiki
where engineers document solutions to tricky bugs, letting future engineers search and
resolve similar issues without repeating the same investigation.

The classic SDLC divides system development into a sequence of phases. Planning establishes
the project's scope, objectives, feasibility, and resource requirements. Analysis gathers and
documents detailed requirements from stakeholders, defining exactly what the system must
do. Design translates those requirements into a technical blueprint, covering the system's

architecture, database structure, and user interface. Implementation (or development) is where
the actual code is written based on the design. Testing verifies that the system works correctly
and meets requirements, catching defects before release. Deployment releases the finished
system into the live production environment for actual use. Maintenance covers the ongoing
period after deployment, during which bugs are fixed, minor enhancements are made, and the
system is kept running correctly.
Each phase in the SDLC produces a specific, tangible deliverable that becomes the input to the
next phase - for example, the analysis phase produces a requirements document that the design
phase then uses as its starting point - which is what gives the SDLC its structured, traceable
nature and makes it easier to track project progress and assign accountability at each stage.
Although often illustrated as a straight, one-directional sequence (sometimes called the
'waterfall' approach when phases strictly follow one another without revisiting earlier stages),
in practice the maintenance phase commonly reveals new requirements or issues that feed
directly back into the planning phase for the system's next release or version, making the
overall SDLC a repeating cycle across a system's full multi-year lifetime rather than a single
one-off project.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Structured and predictable process: Breaking development into clear phases makes it
easier to plan timelines, budgets, and resource allocation accurately.
• Clear documentation at every stage: Each phase's deliverables create a documented
trail that makes the system easier to understand, audit, and maintain later.
• Easier progress tracking: Well-defined phase boundaries make it straightforward for
management to monitor whether a project is on schedule.
• Reduced risk of missed requirements: A dedicated analysis phase ensures
requirements are captured and agreed upon before significant development effort is
invested.
• Facilitates quality assurance: A dedicated testing phase built into the process helps
catch defects before they reach end users in production.
Disadvantages / Limitations:
• Inflexibility to changing requirements: In its traditional (waterfall-style) form, the
SDLC makes it costly and disruptive to accommodate requirement changes discovered
after the analysis phase has concluded.
• Delayed delivery of working software: Users may not see or be able to use any part of
the system until very late in the process, increasing the risk of building the wrong thing.
• Time-consuming for large projects: Completing every phase thoroughly for a large
system can take a long time, during which business needs may have already changed.
• High dependency on upfront documentation quality: If early requirements or design
documents are flawed or incomplete, those flaws propagate through every subsequent
phase.

Fig: The Continuous Agile and DevOps Loop
Explanation:
Agile emerged as a direct response to the rigidity of traditional, sequential development
approaches like the classic SDLC waterfall model. Instead of trying to fully define all
requirements upfront and delivering one large system at the very end of a long project, Agile
breaks work into short iterations (commonly one to four weeks, called sprints), each of which
produces a small, working increment of the system that stakeholders can review and provide
feedback on immediately - allowing the team to adapt direction continuously rather than
discovering misalignment only at the very end.
Within each Agile sprint, a team typically cycles through planning the sprint's goals, writing
code, and testing the resulting increment, repeating this loop sprint after sprint until the product
is complete or the team decides to stop. This tight feedback loop, combined with close,
ongoing collaboration between developers and business stakeholders, is what makes Agile far
more adaptable to changing requirements than traditional sequential approaches.

Explanation:
In the traditional, on-premise ERP model, an organisation purchases ERP software licences
and then installs, hosts, and maintains the entire system on its own servers - requiring
significant upfront capital investment in hardware, as well as an internal IT team to manage
upgrades, security patches, and infrastructure. In the cloud ERP model, the vendor instead
hosts the application, database, and infrastructure centrally, and organisations access it as a
service, typically paying a recurring subscription fee based on usage or number of users.
Most cloud ERP platforms use a multi-tenant architecture, meaning that a single instance of
the underlying application and infrastructure serves many different client organisations
(tenants) simultaneously, with each tenant's data kept logically separated and secure from
every other tenant. This design lets the vendor apply software updates, security patches, and
new features to every customer at once, rather than each organisation needing to independently
plan and execute its own upgrade project.
Users access a cloud ERP system through a standard web browser or mobile application,
connecting over the internet to the vendor's infrastructure - which handles the application
logic, the shared database, and the underlying servers and storage. This shifts the responsibility
for infrastructure capacity planning, uptime, disaster recovery, and much of the day-to-day
system security away from the customer organisation and onto the cloud ERP vendor.
Advantages / Benefits:
• Lower upfront investment: Organisations avoid large capital expenditure on servers
and infrastructure, paying instead through predictable, recurring subscription fees.

organisations rely on for day-to-day decision-making.
SAP implementations at large multinational organisations are typically substantial, multi-year

SAP offers and the scale of organisational change required to adopt it successfully across a
large, complex enterprise.

comprehensive coverage of complex business processes across virtually every industry.

reporting and analytics even on very large datasets.
• Large global support ecosystem: A vast network of SAP-certified consultants,

• Strong industry-specific solutions: SAP offers pre-configured industry variants

• Very high implementation cost and complexity: Large SAP deployments are among

• Heavy reliance on specialist consultants: Successful implementation and

actively predict what is likely to happen next and, in many cases, take or recommend action

sensor and equipment data to warn of likely failures before they occur, demand forecasting
models that improve inventory and production planning accuracy beyond simple historical

robotic process automation that handles repetitive digital tasks such as invoice matching or
data entry without human intervention.

applications is not simply a matter of adding a new software feature: it requires a solid
underlying data foundation from well-integrated core systems (since AI models depend on
large volumes of accurate transactional data), careful change management so that employees
trust and adopt AI-driven recommendations, and clear governance over when a system should
recommend an action to a human versus taking that action automatically.

slides.text:
• Results are highly context-dependent: The business impact of AI-integrated features
depends heavily on the specific organisation's data quality and processes, and may not
generalise directly to other companies.
• Rapidly evolving technology: AI capabilities within enterprise applications are
advancing quickly, so specific case study examples can become outdated within a short
time.
• Understates implementation difficulty: Case studies often focus on the end result
rather than fully conveying the data-quality and organisational-change challenges
involved in getting there.
• Limited transparency into model performance: Detailed accuracy or failure-rate
statistics for the underlying AI models are not always publicly disclosed in vendor case
studies.
Examples:
• Example 1: Predictive maintenance case. A manufacturing company embeds AI￾driven predictive maintenance into its ERP, using sensor data to correctly anticipate
equipment failures and significantly reduce unplanned production downtime.
• Example 2: AI-enhanced customer service. A company integrates a conversational
AI assistant directly into its CRM, allowing customer service agents to resolve routine
queries automatically while escalating only complex cases to human staff.
• Example 3: Automated finance operations. A finance department deploys AI-driven
invoice processing within its ERP, reducing the manual effort previously required to
match invoices against purchase orders and flag discrepancies.
Applications:
• Manufacturing and asset-intensive industries: Applying predictive maintenance to
reduce unplanned equipment downtime.
• Retail and consumer goods: Using AI-enhanced demand forecasting to optimise
inventory and reduce stockouts or overstocking.
• Customer service operations: Deploying AI chatbots integrated with CRM systems to
handle routine customer interactions.
• Finance and back-office operations: Automating repetitive processes such as invoice
matching and reconciliation with AI and RPA.
• Enterprise technology strategy: Informing organisational decisions about which AI
capabilities to prioritise when modernising enterprise systems.
